Latent Projection for Latent Planning

Yoo Sung Jang Affiliation: Stony Brook University    Michael S. Ryoo Affiliation: Stony Brook University
Abstract

Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss–Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)z^{\prime}\mid z\sim\mathcal{N}(Az,\,I-AA^{\top}). Fitting the state dynamics AA therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining AA to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the ℓ2\ell_{2} cost to the kk-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, AA, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost by up to +54.7+54.7 points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

Keywords: Latent World Models, Planning

1 Introduction

Latent world models let an agent plan in representation space. An encoder compresses an observation into a latent representation, a predictor advances that latent under an action, and a planner searches for an action sequence that carries the latent close to the goal. Every part of the loop involves the latent, and learning this representation is a central design choice that varies across latent world models [34, 2, 57, 20, 19].

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) [30], a recipe for general representation learning, are widely chosen for their simplicity: a JEPA predicts the target’s representation from the context’s representation, and that prediction objective is what shapes the representation. Left unconstrained, the representation collapses to a constant, so JEPAs rely on a regularizer to keep the embedding informative. Recent instances of JEPA use regularizers that encourage the embedding to lie in a structured distribution, most commonly an isotropic Gaussian or a variant of it [4, 50, 28].

LeWorldModel (LeWM) [34] builds a latent world model on this recipe, training an encoder and predictor end to end from pixels with a two-term loss: next-latent prediction and SIGReg [4], which pulls the embedding toward an isotropic Gaussian. Similar to many other latent world models [57, 2, 44], LeWM plans by ranking candidate action sequences on the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent.

The simplicity of the cost, however, overlooks two sources of noise in the representation: (i) the regularizer promotes variance in which noise fills the directions carrying no signal; and (ii) the encoder, trained to represent observations, retains content irrelevant to planning [56, 49, 32]. The distance is then measured partly along directions that carry no information about reaching the goal.

Ironically, the same regularizer that injects the noise also gives the structure to repair it. The embedding is driven to be stationary under the transition, and reading the latents as a Gaussian world model in the sense of Klindt et al. [26], we find the noise is not free but pinned to the transition itself: fit the state dynamics and the covariance comes with it. By projecting onto a subspace determined by the covariance, we obtain a representation restricted to the directions that are certain with respect to the state dynamics. In general, the subspace moves under the transition, but we show that it is fixed under a normality constraint on the state dynamics. All of this is post hoc: the only thing we fit is a constrained linear function; the encoder, the predictor, and the planner are untouched.

Our main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Uncertainty measure in a time-invariant basis. Under SIGReg’s standard Gaussian marginal and a Gauss–Markov model, the noise is pinned to the dynamics, z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)z^{\prime}\mid z\sim\mathcal{N}(Az,\,I-AA^{\top}), where each eigenvector carries its own uncertainty. Each step of the state dynamics generally moves that basis. We show that when AA is a normal matrix, the retained subspace is closed under the dynamics and the same basis serves every timestep.

  2. 2.

    A new planning cost. We measure the cost on the subspace spanned by the kk eigenvectors of I−A​A⊤I-AA^{\top} with the smallest eigenvalues: the directions the state dynamics carry forward with certainty. Empirically, planning with this cost delivers large gains in success rate on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, of up to +54.7+54.7 points under a harder planning setting.

2 Preliminaries: LeWorldModel

LeWM [34] is a latent world model that learns the representation and the state-action dynamics together. An encoder ff maps an observation xx to a latent z=f⁡(x)∈ℝnz=f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and a predictor gg outputs the future latent, z^′=g⁡(z,a)\hat{z}^{\prime}=g(z,a), under an action aa.

Training.

The learning is driven by two terms, the predictor loss and the SIGReg loss [4]:

minf,g⁡𝔼⁡[‖g⁡(f⁡(x),a)−f⁡(x′)‖2]+w​ℛSIGReg.\min_{f,g}\;\mathbb{E}\big[\,\big\|g(f(x),a)-f(x^{\prime})\big\|^{2}\,\big]+w\,\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}. (1)

The SIGReg term pulls the latent distribution toward 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I), which prevents representation collapse; it acts on the encoded latents at every step of the trajectory, so zz and z′z^{\prime} are driven toward the same marginal, providing stationarity in transition.

Planning.

Given an initial observation x0x_{0} and a goal observation xgx_{g}, a candidate action sequence a1:Ta_{1:T} is rolled out from z0=f⁡(x0)z_{0}=f(x_{0}) through the predictor, and its terminal latent z^T\hat{z}_{T} is scored by the distance to the goal latent zg=f⁡(xg)z_{g}=f(x_{g}):

𝒞(a1:T)=∥z^T−zg∥2.\mathcal{C}(a_{1:T})=\big\|\hat{z}_{T}-z_{g}\big\|_{2}. (2)

A sampling-based planner [42] ranks candidates by this cost and iteratively refines its sampling distribution toward better action sequences. The cost, however, falls short as a planning signal: distance in the latent space does not measure progress on the task, the regularizer injects noise into the embedding, and the representation also holds details irrelevant to it. This weakness is well recognized [49, 3, 33, 47, 56].

In this work, we take the encoder and predictor as given: both stay frozen throughout, and we modify only the cost (2), replacing the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} distance with one computed after projecting latents onto a subspace that reflects task-relevant dynamics.

3 Transition under a Gaussian World Model

Our objective is to identify the latent subspace that retains clean state dynamics. In this section, we model the latent space such that the state dynamics take the form of a normal matrix, and show that its covariance is pinned by the transition itself. This covariance in turn identifies the subspace: the directions the state dynamics carry forward with certainty.

This follows from Gaussian world model assumptions similar to those of Klindt et al. [26]. By construction of LeWM training, the latent marginals are standard Gaussian and stationary: SIGReg drives the encoded latent toward 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I) at every step of a trajectory. The rest is our modeling choice: we assume the latent sequence is a Gauss–Markov process, and further assume the state dynamics act independently in some orthonormal basis (on lines and planes).

Model (state dynamics under a Gaussian world model). (i) Markov. At every step, p⁡(z′∣z,…)=p⁡(z′∣z)p(z^{\prime}\mid z,\ldots)=p(z^{\prime}\mid z). (ii) Joint Gaussianity. The pair (z,z′)(z,z^{\prime}) is jointly Gaussian. (iii) Stationarity. Both marginals are standard Gaussian: z,z′∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z,z^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (iv) Normality. The state dynamics act independently on orthogonal lines and planes (see Section 3.2).

Klindt et al. [26] prove that LeJEPA-style training [4] recovers the true latent of a Gaussian world model up to a rotation; Zhang et al. [55] extend this to an action-conditioned predictor as the learner. Every assumption above is invariant under rotation, so we read the model as a statement about the true latent, not about a particular embedding.

3.1 The Transition is Linear with Pinned Noise

By the Markov property (i) and joint Gaussianity (ii), the future latent is expressed as z′=m⁡(z)+ηz^{\prime}=m(z)+\eta at every step, where the state dynamics m⁡(z)m(z) are affine and the noise η\eta is Gaussian and independent of zz. Stationarity (iii) centers both marginals, so m⁡(z)=A​zm(z)=Az, and pins the noise covariance to keep the marginals at 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I). As in Klindt et al. [26], we have an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition, now determined by a single matrix AA:

z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)\boxed{\;z^{\prime}\mid z\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\big(Az,\;I-AA^{\top}\big)\;} (3)

Whatever variance is contracted under the transition is refilled with exactly that much noise, keeping the marginal standard Gaussian. Two consequences follow. First, the noise is pinned to the transition: fit AA, and Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} comes for free. Second, since Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0, every singular value of AA lies in [0,1][0,1].

The covariance further tells us where the uncertainty lies. Since the covariance is symmetric, its eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis: I−A​A⊤=U​diag⁡(σ12,…,σn2)​U⊤I-AA^{\top}=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{n}^{2})U^{\top}. Rotating the latent into that basis, z¯=U⊤​z\bar{z}=U^{\top}z, leaves the transition in the same form,

z¯′|z¯∼𝒩⁡(A¯​z¯,I−A¯​A¯⊤),\bar{z}^{\prime}\mid\bar{z}\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\big(\bar{A}\bar{z},\;I-\bar{A}\bar{A}^{\top}\big), (4)

where A¯=U⊤​A​U\bar{A}=U^{\top}AU and the covariance is diagonal, I−A¯​A¯⊤=diag⁡(σ12,…,σn2)I-\bar{A}\bar{A}^{\top}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{n}^{2}). Along this basis the noise is independent, and each direction uiu_{i} carries its own uncertainty σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}. Retaining those of smallest σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} isolates a subspace with clean state dynamics.

3.2 Normality of the State Dynamics

The remaining assumption (iv) states that the state dynamics are normal: the matrix AA satisfies

A​A⊤=A⊤​A\boxed{\;AA^{\top}=A^{\top}A\;} (5)

In the spirit of the independence assumption in Klindt et al. [26], we assume the state dynamics evolve in some basis in an independent manner. A real normal matrix decomposes as A=Q​B​Q⊤A=QBQ^{\top} [23], with QQ orthogonal and BB block diagonal: 1×11\times 1 blocks λ\lambda, each scaling a line, and 2×22\times 2 blocks r​R​(θ)rR(\theta), each rotating a plane by θ\theta and scaling it by rr.11 1 r​R​(θ)=r⁡(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)rR(\theta)=r\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right), a rotation by θ\theta scaled by r≥0r\geq 0. In the rotated coordinates, z¯=Q⊤​z\bar{z}=Q^{\top}z, the transition becomes z¯′|z¯∼𝒩⁡(B​z¯,I−B​B⊤)\bar{z}^{\prime}\mid\bar{z}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(B\bar{z},\,I-BB^{\top}\big), where the mean and the noise are both block diagonal. Unlike in Section 3.1, the transition is block-wise independent: each block is a transition of its own, carrying uncertainty 1−λ21-\lambda^{2} on a line and 1−r21-r^{2} on a plane. Note that we may take Q=UQ=U.

Beyond the independence itself, normality buys us two things.

Shared basis across every horizon.

For any AA, iterating (3) gives the tt-step transition,

z(t)|z∼𝒩⁡(At​z,I−At​(At)⊤),z^{(t)}\mid z\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\big(A^{t}z,\;I-A^{t}(A^{t})^{\top}\big), (6)

but for a non-normal AA the eigenbasis of that covariance generally changes with tt, so the predictable subspace depends on the horizon.22 2 With A=U​S​V⊤A=USV^{\top}, A2=U​S​(V⊤​U)​S​V⊤A^{2}=US(V^{\top}U)SV^{\top}, and that middle V⊤​UV^{\top}U leaves I−A2​(A2)⊤I-A^{2}(A^{2})^{\top} no longer diagonal in UU. Normality provides the equality At​(At)⊤=(A​A⊤)tA^{t}(A^{t})^{\top}=(AA^{\top})^{t}, under which the basis UU of (4) is shared across every horizon. A transition fitted at a different frame skip should then share the basis and differ only in spectrum. Along the basis, the uncertainty grows as 1−λ2​t1-\lambda^{2t} on a line and 1−r2​t1-r^{2t} on a plane. What motivates a horizon-independent basis is discussed further in Appendix A.

Static and motion content, separated.

The blocks distinguish two kinds of predictable content. A 1×11\times 1 block predicts static content: λ\lambda fixes the uncertainty 1−λ21-\lambda^{2} and nothing more, so all it captures is how much of the feature survives the transition. A 2×22\times 2 block predicts motion content: rr fixes the uncertainty 1−r21-r^{2} the same way, and moreover θ\theta captures how the feature moves in the plane under the transition; at θ=0\theta=0 the feature stays put, so the block reduces to predicting static content. Figure 1 illustrates a motion block across transitions.

How much of the latent is motion versus static content is set by a hyperparameter: PP planes and L=n−2​PL=n-2P lines, where nn is the latent dimension. We use the all-planar layout, P=⌊n/2⌋P=\lfloor n/2\rfloor, unless otherwise stated.

4 Latent Projection for Latent Planning

We now turn (3) into a planning cost. The method has two stages: fit the state dynamics AA to trajectories encoded by a pretrained encoder, then use the covariance it determines to decide which latent directions the planner should compare. LeWM’s encoder and predictor stay frozen; planning then runs on them as before, with AA shaping the cost.

4.1 Fitting the State Dynamics

We encode the trajectory data once with the frozen encoder ff, and fit AA to the latent transitions by least squares,

minA⁡𝔼⁡[‖A​z−z′‖2].\min_{A}\;\mathbb{E}\big[\,\|Az-z^{\prime}\|^{2}\,\big]. (7)

Note that the fit is action-free, so AA describes the state dynamics under the policy that generated the data. The fit must respect two constraints: Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} must be a valid covariance, Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0, and AA must be a normal matrix, as discussed in Section 3. We parameterize AA so that both hold by construction; Appendix B gives the full parameterization.

Multi-step fitting.

The tt-step transition is just AtA^{t} (6), and trajectory datasets supply HH future frames. We therefore fit multiple timesteps jointly,

min⁡∑t=1HA⁡𝔼⁡[‖At​z−z(t)‖2],\min_{A}\;\sum_{t=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}\big[\,\|A^{t}z-z^{(t)}\|^{2}\,\big], (8)

so that a single AA has to account for the tt-step transition at every t≤Ht\leq H (Figure 2(a)).

4.2 Planning in the Projected Latent

Ranking action sequences by latent distance is a statement about reachability, and reachability is governed by the state dynamics. Fitting AA recovers those dynamics and their uncertainty measure. Restricting the cost to the certain directions can then sharpen the ranking.

Fitting AA sets the covariance as Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} at no additional cost. Its eigendecomposition

Σ=U​diag​(σ12,…,σn2)​U⊤,σ1≤⋯≤σn,\Sigma=U\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{n}^{2})\,U^{\top},\qquad\sigma_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\sigma_{n}, (9)

gives the basis that the cost will use: the ii-th column uiu_{i} of UU carries noise variance σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}, and the columns are ordered from most to least certain.

We keep the kk most certain directions. Writing Uk∈ℝn×kU_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k} for the corresponding columns, we replace the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost (2) with the distance computed after projecting both latents onto that subspace,

𝒞k(a1:T)=∥Uk⊤z^T−Uk⊤zg∥2,\mathcal{C}_{k}(a_{1:T})=\big\|U_{k}^{\top}\hat{z}_{T}-U_{k}^{\top}z_{g}\big\|_{2}, (10)

where z^T\hat{z}_{T} is obtained by rolling the candidate action sequence forward through the frozen predictor gg exactly as before. Only the cost changes; the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all untouched. Taking k=nk=n recovers the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost, since the projection is then a rotation, which leaves distances unchanged.

The subspace does not depend on the horizon.

The tt-step transition (6) carries noise I−At​(At)⊤I-A^{t}(A^{t})^{\top}. By the normality assumption this equals I−(A​A⊤)tI-(AA^{\top})^{t}, which shares the eigenvectors of Σ\Sigma at every tt (Section 3.2). Only the eigenvalues change, growing monotonically with tt. One basis therefore serves every horizon. For a non-normal AA the basis generally changes with tt, and no single choice serves every horizon. This is what motivates building normality into the parameterization of AA.

5 Experiments

The experiments answer three questions: whether the cost under the projected latent representation improves planning and how it compares to other baseline methods (Sections 5.2 and 5.3); whether the effect relies on the structure the regularizer imposes on the embedding (Section 5.4); and whether the structure imposed on the state dynamics matters (Section 5.5).

5.1 Environments and Planning Setup

We evaluate on six environments: TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench-Cube, Reacher, PointMaze-UMaze, and PointMaze-Medium. For each we take a pretrained checkpoint and keep the encoder and predictor frozen, with per-task details deferred to Appendix C. The state dynamics AA are fit under the parameterization of Appendix B, on the same trajectory data that trained the world model, at frame skip 55 and prediction horizon H=4H=4, for 5050 epochs with AdamW at learning rate 10−310^{-3} and batch size 10241024. The latent dimension is n=192n=192 throughout, and the rank of the projection is swept over k∈{2,4,8,…,128,192}k\in\{2,4,8,\ldots,128,192\} on validation seed 00 to pick the best rank k⋆k^{\star}. Taking k=nk=n recovers the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost that LeWM plans with. We fit AA with 33 seeds {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\} and report the mean and standard deviation of planning success rate. Evaluation is held fixed at test seed 11, so every entry is scored on the same 5050 initial states and goals, matching the evaluation protocol of prior work [34, 57].

We adopt the planning configuration of LeWM throughout: a cross-entropy method (CEM) solver [42] with a planning horizon of 55 steps, our default setting; the exact configuration is deferred to Appendix D. We also evaluate a harder setting with planning horizon 1010, where the choice of cost has a larger effect on success rate.

5.2 Planning under Projection

To answer whether the cost under the projected latent representation improves planning, we plan with 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} (10) at every rank of the sweep. As a control, we project the latent onto a random orthonormal basis of rank kk instead, resampled for each seed. Any gap between the two comes from keeping the informative latent directions. At k=nk=n both recover the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost (2) exactly, since projection onto a full orthonormal basis preserves the distance.

Figure 3 reports the sweep on the validation seed. On most tasks, a small number of ranks already matches what the cost computed on the full basis achieves, and projection onto a random basis behaves similarly. This indicates the latent representation carries a great deal of information irrelevant to planning. Appendix E supports this, reporting the eigenvalues of the transition noise, where the state dynamics are typically uncertain along a large part of the basis. More subtly, our cost matches the full-basis success rate at a lower rank than the random control. The same ordering appears in state recovery (Appendix F), where a linear probe recovers the ground-truth state from the retained directions well before a random subspace of the same size does.

We now turn to where the projection helps. It wins clearly on TwoRoom, PointMaze-UMaze and PointMaze-Medium. The gain is most significant under the harder setting. Projection onto a random basis shows no comparable gain at any rank. On the remaining tasks the gain is marginal: PushT needs the full basis, and Reacher and OGBench-Cube show no such gain over the random control. Planning can fail in three places: the information the task requires may be absent from the representation, the predictor may not advance the latent accurately over the horizon, or the cost may not capture closeness to the goal latent. Our method repairs only the cost, cannot compensate for a failure of the other two, and rests on the model of Section 3, whose assumptions may not hold under contact-rich dynamics.

5.3 Comparison to Other Planning Costs

Our method projects the latent onto the subspace the state dynamics carry forward with certainty. We compare it against other planning cost baselines that run on the same frozen world model:

  • •

    TD-JEPA (frozen) [3] replaces ℓ2\ell_{2} with a learned temporal distance dψd_{\psi}: a quasimetric head predicts how many steps separate two latents, and the planner ranks a candidate by the predicted temporal distance from its terminal latent to the goal. TD-JEPA blends that distance with ℓ2\ell_{2} as (1−α)​dψ+α​ℓ2(1-\alpha)\,d_{\psi}+\alpha\,\ell_{2} and compares α∈{0,0.1,1}\alpha\in\{0,0.1,1\}, where α=1\alpha=1 is the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost. As published the head trains jointly with the encoder and predictor, shaping the representation itself. Here, to make the baseline comparable, we fit only the head, leaving LeWM’s encoder and predictor frozen.

  • •

    PCA is a standard linear dimensionality reduction [25]. We take the covariance of the latents, project onto its top kk eigenvectors, and measure the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The rank is swept over the same grid as our cost, k∈{2,4,8,…,128,192}k\in\{2,4,8,\ldots,128,192\}, and selected the same way. Note that SIGReg drives the marginal toward 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I), whose covariance is the identity; at the optimum PCA reduces to projecting onto a random orthonormal basis.

Both run under the planning setup of Section 5.1, on all six tasks and in both the default and harder settings.

Figure 4 reports the comparison on the test seed. The observation from the validation seed (Section 5.2) holds, with large gains under the harder setting: +36.7+36.7 on TwoRoom, +54.7+54.7 on PointMaze-UMaze and +15.3+15.3 on PointMaze-Medium over LeWM. Among the baselines, TD-JEPA trains its cost with additional supervision, the number of steps separating two latents, while our cost comes purely from the frozen representation. Despite that, the two are comparable: averaged over tasks we are −0.9-0.9 default, −1.7-1.7 harder, both against α=0\alpha=0. PCA also measures the cost on a subspace, but chooses it by variance in the embedding rather than variance in the dynamics, and we outperform it by a greater margin, +3.2+3.2 default and +13.1+13.1 harder.

5.4 Varying the Latent Regularizer

The derivation in Section 3 starts from the latent marginals being standard Gaussian, which SIGReg supplies in training. To test whether the latent projection still works when that structure is weakened or removed, we train three further world models on TwoRoom with the LeWM recipe, replacing only the SIGReg term in (1):

  • •

    VISReg [50] targets the same isotropic Gaussian, enforced with a sliced-Wasserstein term rather than the Epps–Pulley statistic.

  • •

    RDMReg [28, 27] matches the latent to a rectified Laplace — the coordinate-wise ReLU\mathrm{ReLU} of a Laplace — yielding a sparse, non-negative code.

  • •

    Stop-grad [9] uses no explicit regularizer at all: collapse is prevented by detaching the prediction target, and the marginals are unconstrained. With no regularizer weight, we tune the encoder learning rate instead.

To compare the gain across variants, we bring planning success under the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost close together by modulating the regularization strength. Each variant then reruns the sweep of Section 5.2 under the harder TwoRoom setting and is reported at the test seed, everything else held fixed. To measure how well the Gaussian assumption actually holds, we evaluate the Epps–Pulley statistic [12] of SIGReg [4] on held-out latents.

Table 1 reports the outcome. The plain-ℓ2\ell_{2} scores land close but not equal, so we report the gain as a fraction of the headroom each variant has left (gap closed). Every variant with an explicit regularizer term benefits from the projection. The recovery weakens as the latent moves away from the Gaussian: the non-Gaussian target of RDMReg gives up part of the gain (87%87\%), and stop-grad, with no regularizer at all, leaves the latent with no structure for the projection to exploit (0%0\%). The gain reflects how well the embedding carries the Gaussian structure assumed in Section 3.

5.5 Ablating the Structural Constraints

The parameterization imposes structural constraints on AA, and we ablate each component. (i) Positive semidefinite (PSD): the spectrum is kept below 11 in magnitude so that Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} remains a valid covariance. (ii) Normal: A​A⊤=A⊤​AAA^{\top}=A^{\top}A, so one projection basis serves every horizon (Section 3.2). (iii) Motion: the blocks are 2×22\times 2 rotation–scaling planes (Section 3.2); with 1×11\times 1 blocks only, AA reduces to a symmetric matrix, in which case L=nL=n. (iv) Multi-step: AA fits H=4H=4 steps jointly (8) rather than the 11-step transition alone.

Each variant reruns the sweep of Section 5.2 on the harder setting of TwoRoom and PointMaze-UMaze, the two tasks we ablate on, and is reported at the test seed, everything else held fixed; Table 2 reports the result. The full parameterization attains the best success rate, and dropping the normality constraint costs the most on both tasks. The structure drives the gain: an unstructured linear fit improves on LeWM by only +22.0+22.0 on TwoRoom and not at all on PointMaze-UMaze, while the full parameterization of Section 3 gains +36.7+36.7 and +54.7+54.7.

6 Related Work

Planning in latent space.

Model-based planning on a learned latent has a long lineage [16, 43, 21]. We study model predictive control (MPC) [40, 41] in latent space: roll the model forward over candidate action sequences, rank them, execute, replan. PlaNet [18] does this on a recurrent state-space model, ranking rollouts by a learned reward. Nearer to us are models that define the planning cost in representation space: DINO-WM [57] fits a transition on frozen DINO features; V-JEPA 2-AC [2] post-trains an action-conditioned predictor on a frozen video encoder; LeWM [34] trains one end to end from pixels. They rank candidate sequences by the distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent, ℓ2\ell_{2} in LeWM and DINO-WM and ℓ1\ell_{1} in V-JEPA 2-AC, so every latent direction counts the same. In this work, we show that the latent holds content irrelevant to planning, that there exists a clean subspace that carries what matters, and that the distance restricted to that subspace plans better.

Beyond the plain distance.

A recent line of work on latent MPC shares one premise: the latent distance alone is a poor proxy for the reachability the planner needs. The approaches split in two. One line trains the representation so that the plain distance is aligned with what planning needs [54, 37, 49, 47, 33]. The other redefines the cost, commonly regressing a distance on trajectory step gaps as a surrogate for reachability [32, 3]. We keep the latent frozen and train no distance function; instead we fit the state dynamics, a linear function under normality constraints, and compute the cost on the subspace it determines.

Structure in the latent.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) yields representations with emergent properties [8, 7, 38, 53, 22, 35, 39]. Among these, a JEPA learns by latent prediction [30, 1, 5, 34]. Without an anti-collapse term the representation collapses [48, 24]. To remedy this, a stop-gradient with an EMA target was used [15, 9]. Other methods enforce structure on the embedding itself through variance and covariance constraints [6, 52, 13] and, more recently, through an isotropic Gaussian target: SIGReg [4] and subsequent work [56, 50, 29, 58]. Under this target, Klindt et al. [26] prove the learned representation recovers the world’s latents up to rotation, a guarantee unique to the Gaussian. LeWM adopts SIGReg, making its latent stationary under the transition [34]. But the regularizer can harm the representation: the latent is intrinsically low-dimensional, and an isotropic prior on the latent space is an overly strong bias [56]. We instead use the very structure the regularizer imposes to identify the subspace with clean state dynamics.

7 Conclusion

In this work we show that the state dynamics of the latent select the subspace a planning cost should measure on. Under the standard Gaussian marginal SIGReg supplies and a Gauss–Markov model, they are linear and their covariance is pinned by the map itself, z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)z^{\prime}\mid z\sim\mathcal{N}(Az,\,I-AA^{\top}). Constraining AA to be a normal matrix fixes one eigenbasis across every horizon, and the eigenvalues of I−A​A⊤I-AA^{\top} order that basis by the uncertainty the transition leaves along each direction. Measuring the planning cost on the subspace spanned by the kk most certain directions delivers large gains on the 2D navigation tasks. The broader point is that the regularizer preventing collapse both injects the noise and supplies the structure to remove it, and that exploiting that structure yields a clean planning signal without supervision.

Limitations and future work.

We address the cost, but planning can fail in the representation and in the rollout as well, and restricting the cost to a subspace repairs neither. The derivation also rests on two modeling choices: a Gauss–Markov latent sequence, and a normal matrix AA. Future work will explore training a world model that satisfies these constraints. Reachability is also a quasimetric, an asymmetric distance function, while our cost is an ℓ2\ell_{2} distance on a subspace and so symmetric. Our method does fit the state dynamics, however, and they can be used to compute the state occupancy measure [45], a surrogate for reachability. Learning the state dynamics can therefore be a building block for approximating reachability, which we see as an interesting research direction.

Appendix A Why Does Normality Matter?

The cost of Section 4.2 keeps the kk most certain directions of the one-step covariance Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} and measures the distance there. The subspace is chosen once, before planning begins, and applied to every candidate the planner scores. The choice hides a dependence on the horizon. Over tt steps the transition carries noise I−At​(At)⊤I-A^{t}(A^{t})^{\top} (6), and for a general AA the subspace moves with tt. No candidate settles the choice of tt — its remaining gap to the goal is neither given nor fixed. Normality removes the dependence. Every horizon shares one basis and one ordering (Section 3.2), so the subspace from the one-step transition serves them all.

From distance to reachability.

The cost scores the predicted terminal latent against the goal, as a distance. A reachability cost — the state occupancy measure — accumulates likelihood over horizons instead. Under normality every horizon is read in one basis, so the sum over tt factorizes and amortizes, which could be helpful in approximating reachability. We leave that to future work.

Appendix B Parameterization of the State Dynamics

The fit of Section 4.1 must respect two constraints: AA must be a normal matrix and Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} must be a valid covariance, Σ⪰0\Sigma\succeq 0 (Section 3). We parameterize AA so that both hold by construction during the fit.

We take the form from the decomposition A=Q​B​Q⊤A=QBQ^{\top} of Section 3.2. Splitting QQ and BB between the L=n−2​PL=n-2P lines and the PP planes,

Q=[QLQP],B=[BL00BP],Q=\begin{bmatrix}Q_{L}&Q_{P}\end{bmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{bmatrix}B_{L}&0\\ 0&B_{P}\end{bmatrix}, (11)

we parameterize each type of block separately,

BL\displaystyle B_{L} =diag​(λℓ)ℓ=1L,λℓ=vℓ1+vℓ2∈(−1,1),\displaystyle=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L},\qquad\lambda_{\ell}=\frac{v_{\ell}}{\sqrt{1+v_{\ell}^{2}}}\in(-1,1),
BP\displaystyle B_{P} =blkdiag​(rp​R​(θp))p=1P,rp=|up|1+up2∈[0,1),\displaystyle=\mathrm{blkdiag}\big(r_{p}R(\theta_{p})\big)_{p=1}^{P},\qquad r_{p}=\frac{|u_{p}|}{\sqrt{1+u_{p}^{2}}}\in[0,1),
A\displaystyle A =QL​BL​QL⊤+QP​BP​QP⊤,\displaystyle=Q_{L}B_{L}Q_{L}^{\top}+Q_{P}B_{P}Q_{P}^{\top}, (12)

where QQ is the matrix exponential of a free skew-symmetric matrix [31], orthogonal by construction. The free parameters are that skew-symmetric matrix, the LL scalars vℓv_{\ell}, and the PP scalars upu_{p} and angles θp\theta_{p}.

Normality holds by construction.

Each 2×22\times 2 block is a scaled rotation, and R⁡(θ)R(\theta) is orthogonal, so (r​R)​(r​R)⊤=(r​R)⊤​(r​R)=r2​I2(rR)(rR)^{\top}=(rR)^{\top}(rR)=r^{2}I_{2}. Each 1×11\times 1 block is trivially normal. BB is block diagonal with these blocks, so B​B⊤=B⊤​BBB^{\top}=B^{\top}B, and

A​A⊤=Q​B​B⊤​Q⊤=Q​B⊤​B​Q⊤=A⊤​A.AA^{\top}=QBB^{\top}Q^{\top}=QB^{\top}BQ^{\top}=A^{\top}A. (13)
The covariance is positive definite.

The same computation gives

B​B⊤=diag⁡(λ12,…,λL2,r12,r12,…,rP2,rP2),BB^{\top}=\mathrm{diag}\big(\lambda_{1}^{2},\ldots,\lambda_{L}^{2},r_{1}^{2},r_{1}^{2},\ldots,r_{P}^{2},r_{P}^{2}\big),

so

Σ=I−A​A⊤=Q⁡(I−B​B⊤)​Q⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top}=Q\big(I-BB^{\top}\big)Q^{\top} (14)

has eigenvalues 1−λℓ21-\lambda_{\ell}^{2} and 1−rp21-r_{p}^{2}, the latter appearing twice. The squashing in (12) keeps rp<1r_{p}<1 and |λℓ|<1|\lambda_{\ell}|<1, so every eigenvalue is strictly positive and Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0.

Appendix C Environments and Datasets

The evaluation covers six tasks. Four of them — TwoRoom, PushT, OGBench-Cube and Reacher — come from LeWM [34]: the same environments, LeWM’s trajectory data, and the released checkpoints, so the encoder and predictor are frozen throughout and are not retrained here. For PointMaze-UMaze and PointMaze-Medium, we collect the training data, following DINO-WM’s setting [57], and train the world model with the LeWM recipe. Every world model is trained for 1010 epochs. Dataset sizes are given in Table 3. Planning succeeds when the state reached comes within a tolerance of the goal; what that is measured on differs by task.

TwoRoom. A simple continuous navigation task in 2D [44]. The environment has two rooms joined by a single opening, and wall (black) blocks the agent everywhere else. The agent (red) navigates to a randomly selected location in the other room, so it must pass through the opening. The trajectories come from a noisy heuristic that steers to the opening first and to the target once through it.

PushT. A contact-rich 2D manipulation task introduced by Chi et al. [10]. The agent (blue) pushes a T-shaped block (gray) onto a T-shaped goal (green). The agent and block positions are scored together, along with the block’s angle up to its rotational symmetry. The data is the PushT set released with DINO-WM [57], which LeWM adopts.

OGBench-Cube. A 3D manipulation task from the OGBench suite [36]. A robot arm moves a cube to the goal position. We use the single-cube variant. An episode succeeds when the cube ends near the goal, wherever the arm is. The trajectories come from the scripted policy the benchmark provides for data collection.

Reacher. A continuous control task from the DeepMind Control Suite [46]. A two-joint arm reaches for a target. Every joint angle is scored, so the whole arm has to match and not just the fingertip. The trajectories come from an expert SAC policy [17].

PointMaze (UMaze and Medium). A 2D navigation task with physics [14], in two of its maze layouts, run through the Gymnasium-Robotics implementation [11]. A point mass moves through a walled maze, and the action is a force along xx and yy. Only the position of the mass is scored. We collect the training data ourselves, rolling out random action sequences as DINO-WM does [57].

The evaluation start–goal pairs do not come from that random data. On random rollouts the mass often gets stuck at a corner of the maze, so the two states of a pair sit close together; a success rate measured that way comes out inflated. We take the pairs from the D4RL expert trajectories instead, distributed through Minari [51], where the point mass does cross the maze.

Appendix D Planning Configuration

We adopt the planning configuration of LeWM. At each planning step, the CEM solver draws NN candidate action sequences of horizon TT, scores each by the planning cost, and retains the best EE to update the sampling distribution; this repeats for MM iterations, after which the whole optimized sequence is executed before replanning. One predictor step covers cc environment timesteps (the frame skip). At evaluation the goal is drawn Δ\Delta timesteps ahead of the initial state within the same trajectory, and the agent is allowed a budget of bb actions in the environment. Table 4 gives the values for the default and harder settings of Section 5.1.

Appendix E The Spectrum of the Transition Noise

Figure 6 plots the eigenvalues of Σ=I−A​A⊤\Sigma=I-AA^{\top} for the AA fitted to each task, sorted ascending. The eigenvalue σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} is the variance the one-step transition leaves along direction uiu_{i}: at σi2=0\sigma_{i}^{2}=0 the next value is determined, and at σi2=1\sigma_{i}^{2}=1 the transition law along uiu_{i} is the marginal itself, so the dynamics carry nothing forward there.

Every spectrum reaches that ceiling. On TwoRoom, PointMaze-UMaze, Reacher and OGBench-Cube the transition variance is nearer the ceiling than zero over most of the basis, so the state dynamics carry little forward there. PushT stands apart: its spectrum stays low across the greater part of the range.

Appendix F State Recovery in the Retained Subspace

We assume the latent holds the information planning needs. The ground-truth state of the environment can serve as a proxy for that information, so a linear probe from the retained directions to the state tests whether they carry it. We pair cached latents z∈ℝ192z\in\mathbb{R}^{192} with the ground-truth state ss. We keep the kk most certain directions UkU_{k} of the fitted eigenbasis — the same basis the cost projects onto — and fit ordinary least squares s^=W⁡(Uk⊤​z)\hat{s}=W(U_{k}^{\top}z) on 1010k frames, then report held-out R2R^{2} on 1010k frames from disjoint episodes. As a control, we run the same probe on a random orthonormal subspace of rank kk.

Table 5 reports the probe. As the rank grows the retained directions recover the state first, while a random subspace of the same rank lags well behind. What carries the state is the ordering, then, and not the number of dimensions. How quickly the state arrives also tracks the rank planning needs (Section 5.2). PushT and OGBench-Cube are the two tasks slowest to recover, in different ways. PushT climbs gradually, every coordinate improving with kk and none of them arriving early. OGBench-Cube recovers unevenly instead: the planar coordinates arrive at the very lowest ranks, while the two heights and the gripper stay absent until well into the sweep.
